title: Half the fleet, under a third of the electricity: the non-fossil milestone is a capacity milestone
summary: For FY2025-26, non-fossil plant was 53.21% of India's installed generating capacity at 31.03.2026 and supplied 28.96% of the electricity generated over that year — 24.24 percentage points apart. The 50% capacity milestone was announced in July 2025 as reached five years early. The gap is widening, and the widening is the finding rather than any single year. **The figure this record leads on is 10.47 points, FY2014-15 to FY2023-24**, because that window sits inside ONE document: both halves come from facing tables of CEA's General Review 2025, on one universe and one construction, so no join has to be trusted. (Subtracting the two rounded gaps printed here gives 10.48; 10.47 is the rounding artefact resolved on the unrounded ratios.) Extending to the most recent year gives 10.98 in FY2014-15, 21.46 in FY2023-24, 23.52 in FY2024-25 and 24.24 in FY2025-26 — 13.26 points across the full window — but that extension joins a second document and the join is validated ASYMMETRICALLY, which is why it does not lead. The CAPACITY half is validated: at 31.03.2026 the National Power Portal's archive prints 532,739.72 MW against the Executive Summary's 532,739.68, 0.04 MW apart, with an identical non-fossil total. The GENERATION half is NOT validated and cannot be from these documents: the General Review's mode-wise generation table ends at FY2023-24, the Executive Summary's begins at FY2024-25, they share no period, and neither retrieved Executive Summary carries a multi-year generation-by-fuel table against which the join could be checked. Both figures are given because the longer one is more current and the shorter one is more certain, and a reader is entitled to know which is which. Both windows start at FY2014-15 because FY2013-14 is on the imputed side of P-122's basis seam; starting there instead gave 11.77 points, so the seam alone was inflating the widening by 1.30 on the unrounded basis this record leads on, or 1.29 on the printed operands. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this sentence previously gave 1.29 alone, with no basis named. 1.29 is 11.77 minus 10.48 — the printed-operand widening that this same paragraph sets aside in favour of 10.47 — so the figure was derived from the operand the record had just rejected, and the two declarations above cover the widening and the full-window gap but not this third quantity. (Subtracting the two rounded figures printed here gives 24.25. That is a rounding artefact and not an error: 24.24 is the difference computed on the unrounded ratios, and rounding-then-subtracting does not commute with subtracting-then-rounding.)
claimAtLaunch: At COP26 on 1 November 2021 the Prime Minister announced five commitments, of which the first two bear here: 'India will reach its non-fossil energy capacity to 500 GW by 2030' and 'India will meet 50 percent of its energy requirements from renewable energy by 2030.' The updated NDC approved by Cabinet on 3 August 2022 carries the capacity limb as a share — about 50 per cent of cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030, raised from the 40 per cent of the 2015 NDC.
whatHappened: The capacity limb was reached early and the government said so: on 14 July 2025 MNRE announced India had reached 50% of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources 'five years ahead of the target', on a reading of 50.08% against 49.92% fossil at 30.06.2025 — a margin of 0.74 GW on 484.82 GW. By 30.06.2026 the figure was 54.18%. The energy limb has no reporting at all: no document retrieved in this run states progress toward '50 percent of energy requirements from renewable energy', and the nearest published quantity is of a different numerator — the Ministry's own 'share of non-fossil fuels in total generation reached 29.2% in 2025-26 (538.97 BU)' of 1,845.921 BU. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: the generation figure this record pairs with capacity was previously 28.84 per cent. That construction put CEA's Bhutan import inside the denominator and outside the numerator — an import in one and not the other, which is a population mismatch inside a share. Removing it from both sides gives 28.96 per cent, which is also the basis CEA's General Review uses for every earlier year in the series, and the figure this record now carries. Counting the imported hydro on both sides instead gives 29.27 per cent, close to the Ministry's published 29.2. All three are defensible except the one that was here. Two official releases instead announce a '50 per cent of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources' target as a COP26 goal. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this record previously said COP26 'announced no such goal', which is wrong — COP26 is where Panchamrit was announced, including the 500 GW non-fossil CAPACITY goal. The defect is narrower and survives: the 50 per cent limb announced at Glasgow was 50 per cent of ENERGY REQUIREMENTS from RENEWABLE energy, while the 50 per cent of INSTALLED CAPACITY from NON-FOSSIL sources comes from the August 2022 NDC update. The releases fuse element 2's percentage with the NDC's denominator and attribute the result to Glasgow. That substitution is a measurement fact about publishers and is carried in P-123. On CEA's own facing tables the gap between the two shares widened from 10.98 percentage points in FY2014-15 — 31.53 per cent of capacity against 20.55 per cent of generation — to 21.46 in FY2023-24, where capacity was 44.97 per cent and generation 23.51 per cent.
caseFor: The capacity commitment was stated in capacity, measured in capacity, and met in capacity, five years inside its deadline — and the metric was not chosen after the fact: the NDC lodged in 2022 and the 2015 NDC before it both denominate the target in installed capacity, so the government is being held to the arithmetic it published in advance. The underlying build is real and large: renewable capacity excluding large hydro rose from 35,850 MW at 31.03.2014 to 236,525 MW at 30.06.2026, and 50,905 MW was added in FY2025-26 alone, the largest year on the series. A capacity share is also the only quantity a government can directly control — it can procure plant, and it cannot procure wind — so a capacity target is the honest form for a commitment about state action. The generation share lags for a physical reason that no policy can repeal, and it is rising: non-fossil generation reached 29.2% in FY2025-26 on the Ministry's own figure, up from 23.51% two years earlier.
caseAgainst: The two quantities are read as one, and the gap between them is not a technicality but roughly a factor of two. A reader told that non-fossil sources are 'half the nation's grid' — MNRE's own sub-headline — will take it that half the electricity is non-fossil, and under a third is. The milestone itself was claimed on 0.08 percentage points, and it depends entirely on the composition of the numerator: the same release's own second table puts renewable energy proper at 38.08%, the 50.08% being reached only by adding large hydro at 10.19% and nuclear at 1.81%. The target it was measured against reads 'about 50 percent', and nothing in any retrieved document defines what 'about' admits. Most seriously, the one commitment of the five that IS denominated in energy rather than capacity — Panchamrit element 2 — is the only one no retrieved document reports progress against, while two official releases announce the capacity limb as though it were that goal. The quantity that would test whether the energy mix changed is the quantity that goes unreported.

sources.name: CEA, General Review 2025, Table 1.2 (installed capacity, mode-wise, utilities) and Table 1.3 (gross generation, mode-wise, utilities), 1950 to 2023-24
CEA, Installed Capacity (MW) of the country as on 30.06.2026 — 'Total Non-Fossil Fuel' 297,369 MW of 548,858 MW
CEA, Executive Summary on Power Sector, June 2026 — generation by fuel and installed capacity sector-wise
PIB / Prime Minister's Office, 'National Statement by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi at COP26 Summit in Glasgow', 1 Nov 2021 — the Panchamrit text
PIB / Cabinet, 'Cabinet approves India's Updated Nationally Determined Contribution', 3 Aug 2022 — states the updated goals and the 2015 baseline of 40 per cent
PIB / MNRE, 'India's Renewable Rise: Non-Fossil Sources Now Power Half the Nation's Grid', 14 Jul 2025 — the 'five years ahead' claim and the three annexure tables at 30.06.2025
PIB / MNRE, 'India Ranks third globally in Renewable Energy Installed Capacity', 8 Apr 2026 — 283.46 GW non-fossil as on 31.03.2026 and the 29.2 per cent generation share for 2025-26
PIB / Ministry of Power, 'India achieved Historic milestone in power sector', 29 Oct 2025 — the 51.5 per cent figure for 29 July 2025

caveat: The 51.5 per cent figure that circulates as 'renewables met 51.5% of demand in July 2025' is not a monthly or annual energy share. The Ministry of Power release that originates it states 'On 29 July 2025, India reached its highest-ever renewable energy share in electricity generation. That day, renewables met 51.5 % of the country's total electricity demand of 203 GW', and gives its components as solar 44.50 GW, wind 29.89 GW and hydro 30.29 GW. Every operand is in GW, a unit of power; 44.50 + 29.89 + 30.29 = 104.68, and 104.68 / 203 = 51.57 per cent. It is a ratio of simultaneous power readings at one unstated moment on one day, and no energy unit, time of day or data source appears anywhere in the release. A later MNRE release of 8 April 2026 restates the same sentence as 'in July 2025', converting the instant into a month with the numbers unchanged. This record does not use the figure as a generation share and neither should anything citing it.

unmeasured.what: Progress against Panchamrit element 2 — meeting 50 per cent of energy requirements from renewable energy by 2030
unmeasured.why: This is the only one of the five COP26 commitments denominated in energy rather than capacity, and no document retrieved in this run reports progress against it. The two releases that come closest (PIB 2183866 of 29 Oct 2025 and PIB 2250039 of 8 Apr 2026) instead restate the capacity limb and attribute it to COP26. The published 29.2 per cent non-fossil generation share is not this quantity: its numerator is wider than 'renewable energy' and its denominator is generation rather than energy requirements.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Any MNRE, Ministry of Power or CEA statement of renewable energy as a share of energy requirements, with the numerator and denominator named, for any year since 2021.

unmeasured.what: What 'about 50 percent' admits as satisfying the NDC capacity limb
unmeasured.why: The updated NDC's electricity goal is stated as 'about 50 percent' and no retrieved document defines a tolerance in either direction. A 50.08 per cent reading was announced as achieving it; on the same undefined wording 49.5 per cent could be argued to satisfy it and 50.08 per cent argued not to. Whether 'by 2030' means calendar 2030 or FY2029-30 is also unstated in every document retrieved. NO ROUTE IS NAMED DELIBERATELY: this is a gap in a definition rather than in a measurement, so no retrieval closes it — only the target's own author can say what 'about' admits, and until they do the threshold is unfalsifiable in both directions. A wouldFill here would be a placeholder, which enters the verification queue and cannot be worked.

assessmentNote: PARTLY, and the two limbs are scored separately because they are different quantities. The capacity limb — 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, and the NDC's about-50-per-cent share — is delivered ahead of schedule on the metric it was written in, and that is not a grudging concession: the metric was fixed in 2015 and again in 2022, before the result. The energy limb — 50 per cent of energy requirements from renewable energy by 2030 — is commitment state (a), not yet due, and PARTLY is NOT a finding that it has failed; 2030 has not arrived. GROUND NARROWED 2026-08-05. What is scored against the package is one thing only: element 2 is the sole limb of the five with no reporting of any kind, so a reader cannot track it before 2030 whether or not it is met then. THE MISATTRIBUTION IS NOT PART OF THE GROUND AND HAS BEEN MOVED OUT. This record previously also cited two releases restating the capacity limb as a COP26 goal; that is a fact about what PUBLISHERS did, not about what the government achieved, and marking a commitment down for a third party's reporting error confuses measurement with performance. It is now P-123. Note also that the earlier wording said COP26 'did not state' the goal, which was false — Glasgow announced the 500 GW capacity limb; the substitution is between element 2's ENERGY percentage and the NDC's CAPACITY denominator. PARTLY survives the narrowing because claimAtLaunch names BOTH limbs, so the record scores a two-limb package of which one is delivered early and one is untrackable — not a single met commitment discounted for someone else's error. WORKED was rejected because it would score the package on the limb that was measured and stay silent on the limb that was not. FAILED and TOO-EARLY were both rejected: the capacity limb is resolved, so the record is not waiting on time, and it is resolved in the government's favour. THE COMPARISON'S START YEAR MOVED, and this is a correction not a preference: the widening was previously stated from FY2013-14, which sits on the IMPUTED side of P-122's basis seam, where RES generation is normative and higher than metered. That understates the opening gap and overstates the widening by an amount nobody has quantified, and the `breaks[]` contract binds the SERIES and does not reach a derived comparison stated in prose. The claim now runs FY2014-15 to FY2023-24, entirely on the actual-generation basis: 10.98 to 21.46 points. Complements L-0052 rather than duplicating it — L-0052 scores the capacity expansion WORKED on the capacity target and states in terms that 'this record carries no figure for the generation share'. This record supplies that figure.
revisitTrigger: Any published statement of renewable energy as a share of energy requirements, which would make Panchamrit element 2 trackable; or the non-fossil generation share reaching 40 per cent, at which point the gap against the capacity share would be narrowing rather than widening.

title: Coal imports were to stop in FY2023-24 and hit their record that year; production rose 85 per cent
summary: On 18 February 2020 the Minister of Coal said India would stop importing thermal coal from FY2023-24 and that Coal India would produce 1 billion tonnes that year. In FY2023-24 non-coking coal imports — the thermal category the commitment names — were 205.72 million tonnes, the highest in the published ten-year table; Coal India produced 773.81 MT against 1,000. All-India coal production rose from 565.77 MT in FY2013-14 to 1,047.52 MT in FY2024-25.
claimAtLaunch: 'India will stop importing thermal coal from Financial Year 2023-24', Union Minister of Coal and Mines, 18 February 2020, at a Chintan Shivir which also set a '1 billion tonnes (BT) coal production target by Coal India Limited (CIL) by Financial Year 2023-24'.
whatHappened: Neither limb was met and the direction was opposite on both. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this record previously led on total coal imports of 264.53 MT for FY2023-24. That column is TOTAL coal — coking 58.813 plus non-coking 205.718 — and coking coal is metallurgical, not thermal, and not substitutable for geological reasons this record concedes below. The commitment named thermal coal, so the quantity that measures it is the NON-COKING column: 205.72 MT in FY2023-24, against a target of zero, and the maximum of the published ten-year series. The total-coal figure is retained here only as context, not as the evidence: 264.53 MT, also a series maximum. Coal India produced 773.81 MT against 1,000 MT. Imports fell to 243.62 MT in FY2024-25, still 46 per cent above the FY2013-14 level. The objective was restated twice on narrower terms: a March 2024 Strategy Paper moved the horizon to 2030 and the object to 'substitutable' imports, and a January 2026 review reported a 54.17 per cent reduction in 'imported coal for blending' — 5.5 MT against 12 MT — a category roughly 2.3 per cent of total imports. Meanwhile the coal fleet was not idling: PLF of coal and lignite stations fell from 65.56 per cent in FY2013-14 to 54.49 per cent in FY2020-21 and then rose four years running to 69.45 per cent in FY2024-25, above where it started and the highest since FY2010-11. The planned coal build was revised upward twice — the National Electricity Plan of May 2023 put required coal capacity at 259.6 GW in 2031-32 with 19.1 to 27.1 GW of additional build beyond 26.9 GW under construction; by July 2024 the Ministry of Power stated 283 GW and 'additional minimum 80 GW'; by February 2026, 307 GW by 2034-35 and 'additional minimum 97,000 MW'.
caseFor: The objective was availability, not abstinence, and on availability it was delivered: all-India production rose 85 per cent in eleven years, with only one year-on-year fall in the whole series, the COVID year. Coal India's own share fell from 81.73 to 74.56 per cent as captive and commercial mines were opened to competition, so the increase came with a structural liberalisation and not only from the incumbent. Import dependence did fall against the demand it served — imports were 46 per cent higher across a period in which production rose 85 per cent, so domestic coal displaced imports at the margin, and the FY2024-25 fall of 20.9 MT was accompanied by a stated foreign-exchange saving of about $7.93 billion. Coking coal, which India cannot substitute for geological reasons, is a large part of the residual import and no policy could have removed it. A rising PLF on an existing fleet is the cheapest possible way to meet demand growth and avoids capital that would otherwise have been spent on new plant.
caseAgainst: The commitment named a fuel, a direction and a year, and in that year the quantity it named reached its maximum. That is not a near miss: non-coking imports in FY2023-24 were 205.72 MT against a target of zero, and the production limb that was supposed to make the substitution possible came in 226 MT short. No document retrieved acknowledges the miss or restates the FY2023-24 commitment; what appears instead is a different target with a later date and a narrower object, and a progress figure — 5.5 MT of coal 'imported for blending' — drawn from a category two orders of magnitude smaller than the one the commitment was about. The wider point is that the coal system expanded on every measure at the same time as the renewable system did: production up, imports above their starting level, the existing fleet run harder than in 2014, and the announced new-build programme roughly doubled from about 51 GW to 97 GW in under three years. On the Ministry's own retrieved figures new coal is dearer per kWh than firm dispatchable renewables — INR 5.38 to 6.30 against INR 4.98 to 4.99 — and the release stating both says a direct comparison is not appropriate without saying what the appropriate one is.

Coal Controller's Organisation / DGCI&S, Table 8.1, 'Year Wise Import of Coal, Coke & Other Coal Products to India during last Ten Years', FY2015-16 to FY2024-25
Ministry of Coal, 'Company Wise Production of Raw Coal during last ten years (MT)', to FY2024-25
CEA, 'Growth of Electricity Sector in India from 1947-2025', Chart 13 — All India PLF of coal and lignite thermal stations
CEA, National Electricity Plan 2022-32, Volume I (Generation), gazette text — coal capacity scenarios for 2031-32

caveat: The three coal-capacity requirement figures are like for like on fuel scope, and this was checked rather than assumed. The National Electricity Plan's running text calls 259.6 GW 'coal based capacity', which would not be comparable with the 'coal & lignite' of the two later Ministry of Power statements — but the Plan's own Exhibit 5.5a labels that row 'Coal + Lignite' at 259.6, and its highlight xii itemises the same 2031-32 conventional capacity as 'Coal-259,643 MW'. The Plan uses the short phrase for the combined quantity, so no lignite adjustment is warranted and the steps 259.6 to 283 to 307 GW stand at face value. What is NOT like for like is the horizon: the first two figures target 2031-32 and 2032, the third 2034-35, so part of the final step is three additional years of growth rather than a re-rating of the same year. The February 2026 reply also measures its 97,000 MW against installed capacity 'as on 31.03.2023', a baseline nearly three years stale at the time of the reply, and the documents retrieved contain no statement of why that baseline was used.

unmeasured.what: Any acknowledgement that the FY2023-24 thermal-coal-import stop was not met
unmeasured.why: The commitment was stated with a fuel, a direction and a year. The documents retrieved in this run contain no restatement, revision or acknowledgement of that specific commitment after the year passed; the March 2024 Strategy Paper and the January 2026 Year End Review both set out different objectives without referring to it. This is an absence in the documents retrieved, not a finding about intent.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Any Ministry of Coal statement, Parliamentary answer or audit report addressing the FY2023-24 thermal-coal-import commitment after FY2023-24.

unmeasured.what: Whether the 17,360 MW of thermal capacity commissioned since April 2023 counts toward the 97,000 MW additional requirement
unmeasured.why: The February 2026 reply measures its 97,000 MW against installed capacity 'as on 31.03.2023' and separately reports 17,360 MW commissioned since April 2023, without stating whether the second is inside the first. The identified pipeline exceeds the target by 6,845 MW on one reading and falls 10,515 MW short on the other. The document does not resolve it.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Power or CEA statement of the coal pipeline against a single stated baseline date.

assessmentNote: FAILED is scored against the announced objective, which was specific: stop importing thermal coal from FY2023-24, with a named production limb to make it possible. Both limbs were dated, both fell due, and both were missed on the Ministry's own published data — non-coking imports at a series maximum in the target year, Coal India 226 MT short. Under the instrument's commitment states this is (b), due and undelivered, and FAILED is the assessment that follows; the definition covers a measure that did not achieve the objective stated at announcement, which is the case here regardless of the mechanism. REVERSED was rejected because no retrieved document withdraws the commitment — silence is not repudiation, and the later restatements set out different objectives without referring to the earlier one. PARTLY was rejected because neither limb was partially met in the relevant year: the import figure moved away from the target, not toward it. The record's wider material — production, PLF, the doubling of the planned coal build — is context for why the objective failed and is not itself scored; a rise in coal production is not a failure against any objective retrieved, because no document retrieved states an objective to reduce it.
revisitTrigger: Any Ministry of Coal document addressing the FY2023-24 import commitment after the fact; or non-coking coal imports falling below the FY2015-16 level of 159.39 MT, which would make the substitution claim testable on the series rather than on the blending subset.

title: The emissions-intensity limb is the only climate target in the set with a base year — and it is a ratio that can fall while emissions rise
summary: India's updated NDC commits to reducing the emissions intensity of GDP by 45 per cent below 2005 levels by 2030, raised from the 33-35 per cent of the 2015 NDC. It is the only quantified climate commitment in this set that names a base year. On the Ministry's own account the intensity had already fallen 24 per cent from 2005 levels by 2016 — before the target was raised.
claimAtLaunch: India's 2015 NDC committed 'to reducing the emissions intensity of its GDP by 33-35% below 2005 levels by 2030'. The updated NDC of August 2022 raised it: 'Reduce the emission intensity of the GDP by 45% below 2005 levels by 2030.' The Cabinet release approving the update states the same commitment in the Government's own words.
whatHappened: The Ministry's Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy, submitted to the UNFCCC in November 2022, reports the outturn: 'the emissions intensity of India's GDP had already reduced by 24% from 2005 levels until 2016'. That is between 69 and 73 per cent of the 33-35 per cent target depending which end of the band is taken — 24 over 35 is 68.6 per cent and 24 over 33 is 72.7 — banked fourteen years before its due date, and the target was raised to 45 per cent six years after the reading and in the same year as the strategy. 2030 has not arrived and no later intensity reading was retrieved in this run.
caseFor: The limb is the best-constructed climate commitment India has made, and the contrast with the rest of the set is the argument. It names a base year — 2005 — where the 500 GW capacity target, the NDC's about-50-per-cent capacity share and NCAP's 20-30 per cent particulate reduction all name none, and a percentage reduction without a base year is not a computable quantity at all. It names a due date, 2030. It has been reported against with a dated figure from the Ministry's own strategy document rather than left untracked, which is more than the energy limb of Panchamrit has received. And it was RAISED rather than restated when progress ran ahead of it, from 33-35 per cent to 45, which is the opposite of the pattern this phase found elsewhere, where a target moved to a basis that flattered it.
caseAgainst: Emissions intensity is emissions divided by GDP, and a ratio falls whenever the denominator grows faster than the numerator. **A 45 per cent intensity reduction is fully compatible with India's absolute emissions rising over the same period**, and on any plausible growth path it is: the commitment constrains the carbon efficiency of output, not the quantity of carbon. A reader who takes it for a reduction in emissions has read a different promise from the one made. The raise is also less demanding than it looks against the outturn: 24 per cent was already achieved by 2016 on the Ministry's own figure, so against the old band's midpoint of 34 the raise to 45 is an increment of 11 points, and the increment actually outstanding at the moment of raising is not stated anywhere retrieved. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this sentence previously said 'about ten points'. The figure is 11, and the understatement ran in the direction of this very argument — that the raise was less demanding than it looks — which is the direction a loose derived figure should never run. And the reported 24 per cent is a 2016 reading published in 2021 and quoted in 2022 — the most recent outturn this run could retrieve is a decade old.

sources.name: MoEFCC, India's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy, submitted to the UNFCCC November 2022 — carries the 2015 and 2022 NDC wordings and the 24 per cent outturn, itself cited to MoEFCC 2021
PIB / Cabinet, 'Cabinet approves India's Updated Nationally Determined Contribution', 3 Aug 2022 — the domestic announcing act, stating the 45 per cent commitment and the 33-35 per cent it replaced

caveat: Emissions INTENSITY is not emissions. It is emissions per unit of GDP, and it falls whenever output grows faster than emissions do — so this target can be met in full while India's total emissions rise substantially over the same period, and nothing in the commitment constrains the total. This record carries no absolute-emissions series and makes no claim about one; the two quantities must not be read for each other.
assessmentNote: TOO-EARLY, on the value's own definition: the measure is in force, the obstacle is elapsed time, and the evidence that would settle it accumulates with time rather than awaiting anyone's decision. The trigger is 2030 and it has not arrived, so the limb is commitment state (a). NOT awaiting-adjudication — nothing turns on a body outside the enacting authority. NOT no-objective: this is the one target in the phase-15 set that is NOT unfalsifiable, because it names both a base year and a due date, and that is most of what the record is for. NOT contested: the two published figures do not disagree with each other. What the record decides now, and does not defer, is the SHAPE of the commitment — that it constrains a ratio and not a total, and that the outturn available is a 2016 reading. Neither of those becomes clearer by waiting.
revisitTrigger: Any emissions-intensity reading later than 2016 — a Biennial Update Report or National Communication would carry one — which would replace a decade-old outturn. And an absolute GHG emissions series for 2005 onward, which is what would show whether the intensity fall coincided with rising total emissions; this record asserts nothing about that and the question is open rather than answered.

title: Two quantified climate limbs state an absolute tonnage and a date, and neither states the baseline it is measured from
summary: India's one-billion-tonne emissions reduction and its 2.5-3.0 GtCO2e carbon sink are the two climate commitments in this set that name an absolute quantity. Both name 2030. Neither names the quantity it is additional to: the first is measured against a projection that India's own long-term strategy does not publish, and the second is 'additional' to a reference no retrieved document states.
claimAtLaunch: At COP26 on 1 November 2021, Panchamrit element 3: 'India will reduce the total projected carbon emissions by one billion tonnes from now onwards till 2030.' Separately, the 2015 NDC committed 'to create an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3.0 GtCO2e through additional forest and tree cover by 2030', restated in the Ministry's long-term strategy as 'to create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2030'.
whatHappened: No outturn for either limb was retrieved in this run, and for the first no outturn is constructible from anything retrieved. India's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy — the country's own statement of its emissions path, submitted to the UNFCCC in November 2022 — contains no projected-emissions figure against which a one-billion-tonne reduction could be measured: 'projected emissions', 'baseline scenario' and 'reference scenario' each return zero across its 283,363 characters, against positive controls of 'emission intensity' at 3, 'carbon sink' at 5 and '2030' at 51 in the same file and the same form. The four 'business-as-usual' mentions are generic discussion of transport trends and of financial additionality, not a quantified national trajectory. For the sink limb the strategy reports a stock — 'The carbon stock in forests is estimated to be 7,204 million tonnes' — but does not say whether that figure is carbon or carbon dioxide equivalent, while the target is stated explicitly in CO2 equivalent; and 'additional to' returns zero, so the reference the sink is additional to is not stated either.
caseFor: Both limbs are real commitments with real content, and the absence of a baseline in these particular documents is not proof that none exists. A projection may well have been lodged with the UNFCCC or computed inside the Ministry, and the sink target's reference may be fixed in the 2015 NDC's own text, which this run did not retrieve — the instrument's own P-124 records that its NDC evidence is one document removed for exactly that reason. India also does publish the raw materials: forest and tree cover is reported at 24.62 per cent of geographical area and forest carbon stock at 7,204 million tonnes, so the sink limb is measurable in principle from a series that already exists, unlike a counterfactual projection. And 2030 has not arrived; neither limb is late.
caseAgainst: An absolute tonnage without a baseline is not a measurable claim, and the two limbs fail in different ways that are each worse than a missing number. The one-billion-tonne reduction is measured against 'total projected' emissions — a counterfactual, which is not observable even in principle: whatever India emits by 2030, the reduction achieved depends entirely on what the projection said, and no projection is published in the document where one would live. The sink limb is a RANGE of half a gigatonne, so an outturn of 2.6 GtCO2e both meets and misses it depending which end is taken, exactly as NCAP's 20-30 per cent does. It is also 'additional' to an unstated reference, and the only stock figure the strategy offers is in units the target does not use — 7,204 million tonnes of unspecified basis against a target in CO2 equivalent, which differ by roughly a factor of 3.67 if the stock is carbon. **Both limbs will still be unscoreable when their trigger date arrives**, and that is a fact about the drafting rather than about the effort.

sources.name: PIB / Prime Minister's Office, 'National Statement by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi at COP26 Summit in Glasgow', 1 Nov 2021 — Panchamrit element 3 verbatim
MoEFCC, India's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy, UNFCCC November 2022 — the 2015 sink limb, the forest carbon stock, and the absence of any published emissions projection

caveat: The zeroes in this record are statements about ONE document — India's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy — and not about what exists. They were taken with positive controls passing in the same file and the same form, so they are sound as far as they reach, and they reach exactly as far as that document. A projection published elsewhere, or a baseline fixed in the 2015 NDC's own lodged text, would close the gap for either limb without any figure here changing.

unmeasured.what: The emissions projection the one-billion-tonne reduction is measured against
unmeasured.why: The commitment reduces 'total projected carbon emissions', so the projection IS the baseline and without it the quantity achieved cannot be computed from any outturn. India's own long-term strategy publishes no such projection: 'projected emissions', 'baseline scenario' and 'reference scenario' all return zero across 283,363 characters against passing positive controls. This is recorded as an absence in that document, which is the document where a national emissions trajectory would be expected to appear.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Any Government of India publication stating a projected national emissions trajectory to 2030 — a Biennial Update Report, a National Communication, or the NDC's own lodged text.

unmeasured.what: The reference quantity the 2.5-3.0 GtCO2e carbon sink is 'additional' to
unmeasured.why: The target is stated as an ADDITIONAL sink, so the reference is half the arithmetic and without it the target names no level to reach. `additional to` returns zero across the 283,363 characters of the Ministry's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy, and the only stock the document offers — 'The carbon stock in forests is estimated to be 7,204 million tonnes' — carries no unit basis against a target stated in CO2 equivalent, so it cannot serve as the reference even by assumption. REASONING RESTATED 2026-08-05: the kind was chosen as 'the weaker candidate', which is not the schema's axis. The schema's test is WHETHER THE DATA EXISTS, and on that test a treaty instrument's own definitional text is producible: if the 2015 NDC fixes the reference it exists and is published, and this run simply did not retrieve it (P-124). The earlier framing is superseded, the kind is unchanged, and the caution it was reaching for still holds: `never-defined` would assert that no agreed definition exists anywhere, which is a claim about the world this run cannot support: the 2015 NDC's own lodged text was NOT retrieved (P-124 records the substitution), and the reference may well be fixed there. `not-published` claims only that the datum exists in a holder's hands and has not been released in what was retrieved, which is what was actually observed. If the lodged NDC turns out to define it, this entry closes; if it turns out not to, the kind moves to `never-defined` and the finding gets larger.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The 2015 NDC as lodged with the UNFCCC, or any MoEFCC statement of the base year and unit basis for the additional carbon sink.

assessmentNote: RE-FILED 2026-08-05 from `too-early` to `contested`, on an operator instruction to score against the printed definitions rather than around them. THE STATES FIRST, because the two questions are separate and were being run together. COMMITMENT STATE IS (a), and CLAUDE.md settles it in terms: 'a total WITH a date is (a)'. Both limbs carry a total and 2030. Not (b) — the date has not passed. Not (c) — nothing retrieved repudiates them. NOT (d) — (d) requires no date, and forcing these into it to reach `no-objective` would be the stretch the enum rule exists to stop. WHY `too-early` WAS WRONG, stated as the assertions it makes that are false. Its definition reads 'THE OBSTACLE IS ELAPSED TIME AND THE EVIDENCE TIME ACCUMULATES.' For these limbs BOTH clauses are false: the obstacle is a missing baseline, not a missing year, and time accumulates nothing at all — in 2030 these will be exactly as unscoreable as today. Filing them there told a reader to come back and find out, which licenses a wasted revisit, and it is the reason the trigger below is no longer a date. WHY NOT `no-objective`, which the earlier note flirted with. Its own definition forbids it: 'Use where nothing was claimed, not where a claim exists and its outcome is unmeasured — that remains contested (see L-0096).' Two claims were made here, with quantities and a date, and they are quoted in claimAtLaunch. `no-objective` would assert that nothing was claimed, which the record's own face contradicts. WHY NOT `awaiting-adjudication`: no body outside the enacting authority has anything pending. WHY `contested` MAKES NO FALSE ASSERTION. Its definition is 'the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and the record does not choose between them.' That is exactly the position: with no stated baseline, the commitment admits more than one defensible reading OF WHAT IT REQUIRES — a sink additional to 2005, to 2015, or to the year of measurement are different targets, and a reduction against an unnamed projection is as many targets as there are projections. The record chooses none because nothing licenses a choice. AND IT FOLLOWS L-0096 RATHER THAN INVENTING A ROUTE: that record scores a stated deadline whose outcome was never published, and its note says 'What is scored is the documented ACT, not the outcome.' The same is true here — caseFor and caseAgainst below both argue the act of announcing an unbaselined tonnage, and neither depends on an outturn. THE UNSCOREABILITY ITSELF IS NOT IN THE VERDICT AT ALL; it is a measurement fact and it sits in `unmeasured[]` below, which is where a reader looking for the missing datum will find it.
revisitTrigger: NOT A DATE, deliberately — 2030 would guarantee a wasted revisit, because nothing about this record becomes answerable by the calendar. Re-read on either of two events, each of which would change the verdict rather than the elapsed time: (1) any Government of India publication stating a PROJECTED national emissions trajectory to 2030, which would give the one-billion-tonne limb the baseline it is measured against and make it scoreable for the first time; or (2) any statement of the reference the 2.5-3.0 GtCO2e sink is ADDITIONAL TO, with its unit basis, which would do the same for the sink limb. Either converts a limb from unscoreable to merely undue, and at that point `contested` should be revisited because the multiple readings collapse to one. Retrieving the 2015 NDC's own lodged text is the cheapest route to (2) — see P-124, which records that this instrument's NDC evidence is one document removed.

title: Net zero by 2070 is one sentence: a year, and no statement of what is being zeroed
summary: The fifth Panchamrit commitment is a single clause — 'by the year 2070, India will achieve the target of Net Zero'. It carries a date and nothing else: no interim milestone between 2021 and 2070, and no statement of which gases, sectors or land sinks the 'net' covers. It is commitment state (a) on the instrument's own test, and unlike the other quantified limbs it does become testable when its date arrives — provided the scope is settled by then.
claimAtLaunch: At COP26 on 1 November 2021, Panchamrit element 5, in full: 'And fifth- by the year 2070, India will achieve the target of Net Zero.' That is the whole of the announcement.
whatHappened: India's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy, submitted to the UNFCCC a year later, is built around the commitment — 'development choices that ensure growth and development of the economy along low carbon pathways towards net-zero by 2070' — and still does not define it. Searched across its 283,363 characters: any definitional form of 'net zero is / means / defined' returns 0, 'all greenhouse gases' returns 0, 'scope of net' returns 0, against positive controls of 'net-zero by 2070' at 4 and 'carbon sink' at 5 in the same file and form. No interim milestone appears either: 'interim target' returns 0 and '2047' returns 0, and the twelve mentions of 2050 are about DEVELOPED countries reaching net zero early — 'India is justified in seeking that developed countries undertake early net-zero, well before 2050' — or a sectoral encouragement that transport 'will be encouraged to achieve high rates of electrification', not a national milestone. The document does report India's 2016 emissions as 2,838 MtCO2e 'excluding land use and land-use change and forestry (LULUCF)', which is the exact term a NET target turns on and which the commitment does not resolve.
caseFor: A date this distant with no interim target is the normal shape of a net-zero pledge and is not evidence of insincerity: every such commitment made anywhere is a statement about a generation, and India's is accompanied by a published long-term strategy setting out sectoral transitions, which many are not. The endpoint is also genuinely well defined in a way the other quantified limbs are not — net zero has an established meaning in the international framework India is party to, and the quantity that would settle it, national net emissions, is already measured and reported. The absence of a scope statement in one document is not proof that no scope is settled. And the strategy makes an equity argument on the record rather than leaving the timing unexplained: India's per capita emissions are 2.46 tCO2e against a global average of 4.79, and its historical contribution about 4 per cent, which is offered as the reason a 2070 date differs from a 2050 one.
caseAgainst: Nothing about this commitment falls due for forty-nine years, and nothing in it can be tested before then. There is no interim target of any kind — not a decade, not a sector, not a percentage — so a reader in 2026, or 2046, has no published quantity to hold it to and no way to distinguish a government on track from one that is not. The scope is also unsettled in the only document that could settle it, and the gap is not academic: India reports its own emissions EXCLUDING LULUCF, and whether land sinks count is the difference between a target requiring the elimination of fossil emissions and one requiring far less. A 'net' target whose net is undefined is a target whose difficulty is undefined. On the instrument's standing test — could a single document, if it turned up tomorrow, falsify this? — the answer is yes, and that is the honest limit of what is asserted here.

sources.name: PIB / Prime Minister's Office, 'National Statement by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi at COP26 Summit in Glasgow', 1 Nov 2021 — Panchamrit element 5 verbatim

MoEFCC, India's Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy, UNFCCC November 2022 — the strategy built on the commitment, its 2016 emissions figure excluding LULUCF, and the absence of any scope definition or interim milestone

unmeasured.what: What India's 'Net Zero' covers — which greenhouse gases, which sectors, and whether land sinks (LULUCF) count toward the net
unmeasured.why: The commitment is stated as a net target and the net is what decides its difficulty. The retrieved documents do not settle it: no definitional statement of net zero appears in the Ministry's long-term strategy, and the same document reports India's own emissions EXCLUDING LULUCF, so the one accounting choice that matters most is made in the reporting and not in the target. REASONING RESTATED 2026-08-05: the kind was chosen as 'the weaker candidate', which is not the schema's axis. The schema's test is WHETHER THE DATA EXISTS, and on that test a scope decision for a lodged international target is producible on the same reasoning: if India has fixed which gases and whether LULUCF counts, that exists in a holder's hands. The earlier framing is superseded, the kind is unchanged, and the caution it was reaching for still holds: `never-defined` would assert that no agreed definition exists, which is false — the international framework India is party to has one — and what was actually observed is that the documents retrieved do not state which scope India adopts. If a scope is fixed in a document not retrieved here, this entry closes.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Any Government of India statement of the gas coverage and LULUCF treatment of the 2070 net-zero target — a Biennial Update Report, a National Communication, or an updated NDC.

unmeasured.why: Without one, no year before 2070 produces a test, and the commitment's progress is unfalsifiable for forty-nine years even though its endpoint is not. Searched the long-term strategy: 'interim target' 0, '2047' 0, and every 2050 mention is either about developed countries reaching net zero early or a sectoral encouragement rather than a national milestone, each read in context. reasonKind CORRECTED 2026-08-05 from `not-published` to `not-collected`, on the schema's own test of whether the data exists: a milestone that has never been announced is not a figure sitting unreleased in a holder's hands — if the Ministry were compelled tomorrow it would have nothing to produce, because the thing missing is a policy decision and not a measurement. `not-published` asserted producibility under compulsion and that assertion was not supported. This is an absence in the documents retrieved, not a finding that no milestone was ever contemplated.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Any published Indian milestone, sectoral or national, between the announcement and 2070 — a dated interim emissions target, or a sectoral net-zero date.

assessmentNote: COMMITMENT STATE IS (a), AND THE TEST WAS APPLIED TO THE PRINTED DEFINITION RATHER THAN TO THE INTUITION. CLAUDE.md settles it in terms: 'a total WITH a date is (a)'. Net zero by 2070 carries a date, so it is (a) with trigger 2070. IT IS NOT (d), and the temptation ran both ways here. (d) requires 'a total with NO date, no phasing and no annual target' — three conditions, and this fails the first. STATE.md warned against forcing it TO (a) merely because a year is named; the answer is that the year is not the reason, the printed carve-out is, and the same carve-out is what put L-0224's limbs in (a) too. Forcing it to (d) to reach `no-objective` would have been the same stretch in the other direction. `too-early` IS EARNED HERE AND WAS NOT IN L-0224, AND THE DISTINCTION IS NARROWER THAN THE EARLIER NOTE MADE IT — IT IS ARGUED HERE RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The objection is fair: this record establishes that the scope of 'Net Zero' is undefined in the retrieved documents, and by L-0224's own reasoning an undefined rule for scoring defeats the claim that time accumulates the evidence. THE ANSWER IS THAT THE TWO RECORDS FAIL AT DIFFERENT PLACES. L-0224's target LEVEL cannot be computed at all: a reduction of one billion tonnes against 'total projected' emissions has no value, on any boundary, because a counterfactual projection is not an observable quantity and no measurement ever produces one. **Here the target level IS specified — zero net — and only the BOUNDARY is unfixed.** The quantity that would settle it exists and is measured annually: the same strategy reports India's 2016 emissions at 2,838 MtCO2e excluding LULUCF, so a reading exists today on at least one boundary and another exists including it. The ambiguity is about WHICH of two observable series counts, not about whether any observable series exists. **So both of `too-early`'s assertions hold: the obstacle is elapsed time, and the evidence does accumulate — two candidate readings are accumulating right now, and at 2070 both will exist.** WHAT THE VALUE DOES NOT SAY, and what this note therefore says instead: time alone is NOT sufficient. Scoring also needs a boundary statement, which is a definitional act available at any moment and is recorded as an absence below rather than folded into the verdict. A reader must not take `too-early` here to mean the record resolves itself by waiting. The difference from L-0224 is that waiting plus one definitional statement settles this one, while no combination of waiting and definition settles that one. That value asserts two things: the obstacle is elapsed time, and the evidence time accumulates. For L-0224's limbs both are FALSE — the obstacle there is a missing baseline and no amount of time supplies one, which is why that record was re-filed `contested` today. For net zero both are TRUE: the obstacle is that 2070 has not arrived, and national net emissions are already measured and reported annually, so the evidence genuinely does accumulate toward an endpoint that is well defined internationally. The two records are the same shape of announcement and take different values for a reason that can be read off the definitions. WHAT IS UNSCOREABLE HERE IS NOT THE VERDICT BUT TWO MEASUREMENT FACTS — the undefined scope and the absent interim milestone — and both sit in `unmeasured[]` rather than in the assessment, which is where a reader looking for them will find them. CONFIDENCE IS MEDIUM: the finding rests on absences in one document, and a scope statement published elsewhere would narrow it.
revisitTrigger: Any Government of India statement fixing the gas coverage and LULUCF treatment of the 2070 target, which would settle what is being zeroed; or the publication of any interim milestone before 2070, which would give the commitment its first testable moment and would move this record off `too-early` for a reason other than the calendar. A revisit on the date alone is not useful before either happens.

title: A rule guarantees no renewable capacity is backed down; the plan built on it projects that some will not be absorbed
summary: The Must-Run Rules of October 2021 are described by the Central Electricity Authority as ensuring 'that no RE capacity is backed down'. The same authority's National Electricity Plan projects that about 1 per cent of renewable generation will not be absorbed in 2026-27 and around 3.3 per cent in 2031-32 — and that on a different assumption about how far coal plants can turn down — 40 per cent minimum technical load against 55 — those figures fall to 0.09 per cent and 1.29 per cent respectively. CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this sentence previously gave the 2026-27 variant alone. That is the same truncation corrected in whatHappened two batches earlier and never carried here, and the omitted half is the one that weakens this record's own emphasis: the assumption moves the near year 11.11x and the far year only 2.56x. No measured figure for either backing-down or non-absorption appears in CEA's principal statistical publications.
claimAtLaunch: 'Ministry of Power has notified Electricity (Promotion of generation of Electricity from Must-Run Power Plant) Rules, 2021 on 22.10.2021. This rule ensures that no RE capacity is backed down. This will ensure that the consumers get green and clean power and secure a healthy environment for the future generation.' — National Electricity Plan 2022-32, Volume I.
whatHappened: The Plan's own modelling does not carry the guarantee through. It states: 'It has been observed that about 1% of RE based generation may not be absorbed during the year 2026-27 while around 3.3 % of the RE based generation may not be absorbed during 2031-32.' **AND THE FIGURE MOVES SHARPLY ON ONE MODELLING ASSUMPTION, WHICH THE DOCUMENT STATES ITSELF:** 'Studies carried out are at 55% Minimum technical load but CEA regulation has been brought out as per which 40 % Minimum technical load can be achieved, considering 40% minimum technical load the RE based generation not absorbed will decrease to 0.09% and 1.29% in FY 2026-27 and 2031-32 respectively.' So both years carry a second variant, on a minimum technical load 15 points lower — 55 per cent to 40. **CORRECTED 2026-08-05: this record previously quoted the sentence truncated at '0.09%' and described the sensitivity as an eleven-fold range, full stop.** That is right for 2026-27, where 1 per cent against 0.09 is 11.11x and a difference of 0.91 points — and it is NOT the whole picture, because the 2031-32 pair is 3.3 per cent against 1.29, a ratio of 2.56x and a difference of 2.01 points. **ON THE RATIO the assumption dominates the near year and much less so the far one: 11.11x against 2.56x. ON THE ABSOLUTE DIFFERENCE THE ORDERING REVERSES — 0.91 points against 2.01, and the far year moves by more.** Which measure governs, stated rather than chosen: this record's claim is about whether a published figure is a forecast or an artefact of a modelling choice, which asks how much of the quantity survives the assumption. That is a proportional question and the ratio answers it, so the ratio governs HERE. It does not govern the planning question. How much energy is at stake is an absolute quantity, and on that reading 2031-32 is the year that moves more — on a generation base this record has not retrieved and therefore does not size. **The ordering claim is true on one measure and false on the other, and the correction that introduced it named neither. That is the same class as the truncation the correction was written to fix**, one batch later and in the sentence doing the fixing. The truncation dropped the half that weakens the point this record was making; the unstated measure kept the half that flatters it. The draft carried a third value: a comment in the Plan's own consultation table quotes 'about 3.48 % of RE based generation may not be absorbed during the year 2026-27' and asks for the 2031-32 figure, answered 'The value included in the Final NEP'. Storage is planned against this: Exhibit 5.5a puts battery storage at 38.71 to 67.04 GW and 193.55 to 335.2 GWh across the five scenarios for 2031-32.
caseFor: The rule and the projection are not in conflict on their own terms, and reading them as one is the easier mistake. The Must-Run Rules bar a discom or load despatch centre from INSTRUCTING renewable generation off the system for commercial reasons; the Plan's 'not absorbed' is a modelled system outcome in hours when demand cannot take the energy at any price and thermal plant is already at its technical floor. A rule about instructions and a projection about physics can both hold. The projection is also small and shrinking under a better assumption — 0.09 per cent at the 40 per cent minimum technical load that CEA's own regulation now permits — and the Plan pairs it with 38.71 to 67.04 GW of storage precisely to absorb what would otherwise be spilled. Publishing a projected non-absorption at all, in the document that also states the guarantee, is disclosure rather than contradiction.
caseAgainst: A guarantee stated without qualification — 'no RE capacity is backed down' — sits in the same volume as a projection that some will not be absorbed, and nothing in either text reconciles them for a reader. The distinction the case for relies on is real but is NOWHERE DRAWN IN THE DOCUMENT: it does not say that non-absorption is not backing-down, and a reader is left to construct the reconciliation. The eleven-fold assumption sensitivity is the sharper problem — eleven-fold being a RATIO, which is the measure this particular argument turns on and not the one that governs how much energy is at stake (see whatHappened): a planning figure that moves from 1 per cent to 0.09 per cent on the minimum-technical-load assumption is not a forecast of curtailment so much as a statement about the model, and the Plan reports the higher figure as its headline while noting the lower one. And the whole question is unmeasured — **CEA's three principal statistical publications contain no curtailment figure at all**, so neither the guarantee nor the projection can be checked against what actually happened in the five years the rule has been in force.

sources.name: CEA, National Electricity Plan 2022-32, Volume I (Generation), gazette text — the Must-Run Rules statement, the non-absorption projections, the minimum-technical-load sensitivity, and Exhibit 5.5a's storage scenarios
CEA, General Review 2025 — checked for a curtailment measure and carries none
CEA, Executive Summary on Power Sector, June 2026 — checked for a curtailment measure and carries none

caveat: 'Not absorbed' and 'backed down' are treated as distinct quantities throughout this record and must not be read as synonyms. Backing down is an INSTRUCTION to a generator; non-absorption is a modelled system outcome. The Plan uses only the second and the rule addresses only the first, and no retrieved document states the relationship between them. Where this record sets them side by side it is to show that the relationship is unstated, not to assert that the projection contradicts the rule.

unmeasured.what: Renewable generation actually curtailed or backed down, in any year since the Must-Run Rules took effect
unmeasured.why: The rule has been in force since 22 October 2021 and the question is measurable — a grid operator necessarily knows how much generation it instructed off the system — but no figure appears in CEA's principal statistical publications. Searched the General Review 2025, the Executive Summary for June 2026 and the Executive Summary for March 2026 for 'curtail', 'backed down', 'not absorbed' and 'must run': **zero in all three documents, against a positive control of 'generation' returning 192, 33 and 34 in the same files and the same form.** So the absence is checked in the documents that would naturally carry it, not merely unlooked-for. reasonKind is `not-published` on the data-existence test: the despatch instructions exist in the grid operator's hands and are producible under compulsion, which is a different thing from never having been gathered.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Any Grid-India or CEA series of renewable energy curtailed or backed down, by year; or a state load despatch centre's published backing-down instructions.

assessmentNote: CONTESTED, and the value is reached the same way L-0224's was — by the route `no-objective`'s own definition prescribes: 'Use where nothing was claimed, not where a claim exists and its outcome is unmeasured — that remains contested (see L-0096).' A claim exists and is quoted in claimAtLaunch; its outcome is unmeasured. The two cases below both argue the DOCUMENTED ACT — a guarantee and a projection published in one volume without a stated relationship — and neither depends on an outturn, which is L-0096's construction. `too-early` WAS REJECTED AND THE ASSERTIONS IT WOULD MAKE ARE FALSE: its definition requires that the obstacle be elapsed time and that the evidence accumulate with time, and here **five years of evidence already exist and are simply not published** — the rule took effect in October 2021, curtailment is measured by whoever instructs it, and no year of it has been released. Time has already passed and produced nothing a reader can see. `no-objective` was rejected because an objective was stated. `failed` and `worked` were both rejected because **nothing measured is available to score either way**, and scoring an outcome on a projection would treat a model as a measurement. CONFIDENCE IS MEDIUM: the projections are firmly established from the Plan, but the record's central claim is about a relationship two documents leave unstated, and a reconciliation published elsewhere would narrow it.
revisitTrigger: Publication of any measured curtailment or backing-down series, which would convert this from a contest between two documents into a measurable question; or any official statement reconciling the Must-Run guarantee with the Plan's non-absorption projection. The arrival of 2026-27 is NOT a trigger — the projection for that year is already published and the measurement that would test it is not.
